beats.say: A razor sells itself. And the blades never stop.
Buy the handle, get a single blade.
Buy the handle, get a starter pack of blades.
Buy the handle, get a subscription of blades forever.
In 1904 they sold 90,884 razors but 123,648 blades. Looks endless.
But it does a job: it forces repeat purchases.
Every razor sold creates a customer who must keep buying blades.
The 1903 launch sold only 51 razors and 168 blades - a tiny repeat base.
By year two the blade count dwarfs the razor count, proving the model.
You see it everywhere. A coffee shop sells a machine for $200 and a cartridge refill for $30 each month.
A gym offers a treadmill for $500 and a maintenance plan for $25 monthly, while a cheap bike costs $150 outright.
The recurring plan feels cheap because the hardware price looks like a one-time deal.
If a product separates a core tool from consumables, expect the consumable to be the real profit. Follow for more.
